Name: Alan Mellor
Question: What’s the best way to grasp object oriented programming?
Answer: (from my book Java OOP Done Right) I think of all the objects as little people at work, each one having a job to do. Each one knows how to do their job, and has all the reference books and supplies they need to do it. So we might have a writer, who writes a letter. This letter is then handed to a postman. The postman drives the letter to a sorting office. The sorting office has inside it a big map of postcodes, and on that map each postcode has a little pin with the name of another postman, who is responsible for delivering the letters. The sorting office hands over the letter to the correct postman, who delivers it to a reader. The writer does not tell the postman how to deliver the letter. Nor does the writer ask the postman anything at all about how the delivery will be done. Each person does their own job, without interference. This is the essence of OOP. I have just described encapsulation - which is the sorting office having a map of postcodes and postmen. Nobody else needs to see that map - it is private data. I’ve also described object messaging. The writer object sends a ‘post this’ message to the postman object. This is also object collaboration. I’ve described the single responsibility principle. Each object does it’s own part of the job. But just that piece; the writer object does not attempt to help the postman. They split up jobs. In code, you might have something like this: And then a process would happen: sorting office looks up the right delivery postman for the postcode W12 8QT, and calls: This is very roughly the essence of OOP. You split a complex job up into small, self contained pieces. And I think of it as little people, who have enough private knowledge to do a small job very well. The big job is done by having many of these little people work together to do their parts. I’ve turned this into a book at Java OOP Done Right which covers how I like to get the best out of OOP in Java, using SOLID principles, TDD and more. Basically, all the stuff I use everyday to create clean, high quality OOP code.

Question: I see some C programmers switching to C++ but still coding in C style or not fully using C++? Are the two programming paradigms too difficult to switch?
Answer: There are some huge differences between procedural programming and object-oriented programming. The biggest one is the idea of runtime polymorphism, supported by virtual member functions in C++. C has no direct equivalent. It has the net effect of turning your call stack upside down. Instead of one function calling another function, we have something calling … we don’t know what exactly. The benefit of this is that we can design a system that can call any compatible function, not just a single one. This allows us to get rid of a lot of conditional statements. It also allows us to write code that can have new functionality added, without changing the existing code. All of that is possible in C (using struct and function pointers). But it does not have that direct support in the C language itself, so it is perhaps less often used. That’s the learning curve going from procedural C to object-oriented C++.

Question: How do you find a potential difference across a circuit with a reversed biased diode and a resistor?
Answer: If it is your bog-standard silicon diode, reverse biassed it will conduct no current. So the entire supply voltage will be found across the diode, with a zero volt drop across the resistor. But if the diode is a Zener diode, it gets more complex. If the supply voltage is higher than the Zener breakdown voltage Vz (so eg 5.6 volts for a 5v6 Zener), you will get Vz across the diode. That will leave the (supply voltage - Vz) across the resistor, and whatever current running through both the resistor and the zener diode. If it is a photodiode, then in the dark, the diode does not conduct and you get the full supply voltage across the diode, 0 volts across the resistor. As the light intensity increases, current starts to flow through the diode. You get voltage appearing across the diode, and less voltage across the resistor.

Question: What is the most difficult concept to understand in the programming language Go?
Answer: We teach some Go courses, including one called “Go in a day” for existing devs, and the top challenges are: Concurrency is hard generally. It messes with our brain. “Con is currenc hard! y” Go provides traditional tools like mutexes and atomics to manage this, but they are not the preferred approach. Goroutines with channels are the flagship Go feature. Figuring out how to avoid the data races between the main goroutine, providers and consumers is always challenging. For kicks, there is a nuance to where you Add() to a waitgroup that most of us get wrong. Static types are not hard, but many trainees now come to us with basic experience of a single language, either JavaScript or Python. So it takes a little time to grasp not just throwing any old thing into a variable. It’s not challenging for anyone, but it does cause a little friction. Method receivers can be either pass by-value or by-reference. That makes sense. But then it’s not quite as you expect it to work. You get compiler errors saying your object is the wrong sort for that receiver. Which makes no sense to me; just take your copy or pass the original. I don’t really care what sort it is. Again, this (on my part) just comes from a misunderstanding of Golang’s goals. I think it is like C++ const - and it never was. Pointers are easy when you know how, and baffling before that point. But you need to understand them in Go, or parts of your program that you think “should work” simply don’t do anything. Your result value will have been discarded. Local variable scope here refers specifically to returning a pointer to local variable. This one unearths the C programmers. In C or C++, dereferencing a returned pointer to a local we expect to crash the system. In Go, some fancy magic happens where that local is silently moved to being not-local, where it is safe to return a valid pointer to it. Go has the idiom where a lowerCase name is privately scoped but an UpperCase name is public. This causes especial hilarity when using JSON marshalling of structs, only to discover that no data gets sent out. You had made the names lower case. The fix is to upper case them, and that makes no sense at all at first. Packages paths also are fine, but work the way they work. The path does not work like an OS file path, with the slashes and dots, it’s relative to the name of the Go module. Another thing that is easy, but often takes many mistakes before you internalise the approach. Go is a good language that I like a lot. But like every language, you have to work the Go way - Go will not work your way ;)

Question: Why do private and methods variables exist in OOP? Couldn't you just avoid using code that would access the variables?
Answer: You get private in many languages even non OOP ones. Marking something as private does a few things: I got sold on this idea when at work in an embedded software job. The change was to make the display flash more quickly for a certain kind of error. The change was made. The result was a quicker flash AND losing all the stored configuration data of the machine. Oops. This happened because a global variable had been used as the flash timer. A different change then used that same variable to control the data write timing. At the time, it was a perfect match in timing. Speeding up the display - and so the write timing - violated the maximum write speed. It took ages to track that down. None of the code appeared to be wrong. Nobody thought they had even touched the config storage code. This should never have happened. Those two disparate features should never have been coupled together. But the variable was not private. So it was possible to couple them. Without the full context of knowing the whole system, it was a mistake waiting to happen. Using a private flash timer fully encapsulated in the display module would have prevented this, and made the code more clear to a human reader.

Question: Computer Science: Why is recursion more elegant than iteration?
Answer: It isn’t. It really isn’t. For the majority of purposes where you have a bunch of things and want to iterate over them and have code that clearly shows you are iterating over them, then iteration is more elegant than recursion. If you want to abstract away from that iteration, and have code that clearly reads “Here are all the things: transform them into this new thing”, then a functional mapping approach is the most elegant. Question: Why is OOP called real world programming?
Answer: An early approach to OOP (Abbott, 1983 if I recall) was to use objects to model the real world. This follows the 1960s early OO language Simula, which was intended to help with simulations of real world things. The idea was to decide which real world objects to model. You would take an ordinary English description of some problem, and look for nouns and verbs in that text. Nouns would be a candidate for objects; these are usually ‘things’ in the real world. The verbs are ‘doing’ words. Verbs represent behaviours that those things do. So verbs became candidates for methods on the objects. A lump of text describing a Student Exam system might have the following nouns: a Student, a Course, an Exam and a Grade Record. We would create objects of these types. We would then decide what behaviours these objects needed to model. An exam might be taken by a Student. Perhaps this suggest a ‘take’ method, or maybe a ‘begin’ or ‘sit’ method. It might then run through a list of questions, get input and check answers. This might result in a grade. The objects would store data needed to support these behaviours. Clusters of objects would collaborate by calling methods on each other. A program is then a set of objects created at run time, each one modelling a specific aspect of a real world problem. It’s still a useful approach. These days, we’ll also add some objects to represent specific technologies, data formats, rules, policies and more. Some kinds of object are common to many programs, giving rise to Design Patterns. The ‘real world’ aspect relates to that modelling of recognisable parts of the world we live in.

Question: How do I design a USART protocol with IC 74194 4-bit binary?
Answer: That chip is a 4 bit shift register. So you load in 4 bits of data, it shifts them out one at a time over a serial line. It’s bidirectional, so you can use it at the receive side to shift bits in and read out 4 bits parallel. I’ve only ever designed simple serial protocols. They seemed to need these things: One I worked on was for serial control of machinery. It had a data frame like this [02][address] [13 bytes data][checksum byte] The 02 byte signalled the start of the frame. The next byte was a machine address. You could number machines 1–255 and address them individually. You could broadcast to all using address 0. Following this address was the payload data. That had its own structure to suit the machine being controlled. There were single bits to signal STOP, RUN and so on. There were parameter values such as a 16 bit speed control. The payload was fixed length, so you could always expect 13 bytes of data. Following the payload was a checksum byte. This helps figure out if the data was corrupt. When you send the data, you compute the checksum and send it. At the receiver, you read in the data, re-compute the checksum and compare to the one sent. They should be identical - else assume the received data is invalid. As networks can stop working at anytime, each byte had a maximum time in which it could be sent. As soon as that time passed, if no further byte was received, the message would be discarded. New bytes would be read until finding the 02 start marker. This would trigger a new ‘expect valid message’ state. You can see how these ideas addressed the four concerns. You could devise something similar. Mapping this into the IC you mention involves chunking up into 4 bit pieces and sending 4 bits at a time down the line. Instead of my byte oriented protocol, consider basing your around 4 bit quantities. At the IC level, you’ll probably need start bits and stop bits to help synchronise things. There are some details about sampling bits on the recover at 16 times your transmission bit rate and taking a majority vote. There are some electrical details about cable length, noise immunity, maximum bit rate. I’ll just wave my hand at this point though ;)

Question: Are DI frameworks like Spring applicable to desktop applications (e.g. in Java)? They noticeably increase startup time (irrelevant in server apps), but DI is still a separate responsibility.
Answer: DI is a technique that doesn’t necessarily take any time. If we use constructor injection, then create all our objects ourselves, and simply wire them up as we create, the time taken is that of the number of new statements. It’s pretty instant. Where Spring takes the time, I think, is when we component-scan. This trawls through all the class files (using reflection, I expect) looking for possible links between an autowire target and a suitable component supplier. Then it figures out a dependency graph. Then it creates all the objects (reflection again, must be) and wires up. There is a lot more work for the Spring run time there, to make less work for the programmer. DIY DI reverses that. So if we want fast startup times, we can avoid Spring DI/IoC and do it ourselves. We can still use much of the rest of Spring as library components.

Question: What helped you become good at programming (with focus on C language and physical computing)?
Answer: Mostly practice. Once I got past basic syntax, it was helpful to write a lot of programs of growing complexity. Some of these were real stretch goals, where I had no clue at the outset how I would achieve them. As I grew out to write bigger programs, I started noticing that my programs became harder to add to. They were hard to understand. Changes would often have surprising effects I wasn’t expecting. I noticed I became less sure just looking at the code if it would “work” or not. I hadn’t even realised I never tested for all scenarios the code might be used in; just the few that came to my mind. That led to more learning about structuring software, how we design components and decompose systems, testing. Eventually that led to things like OOP, Design Patterns, Test-Driven Development and Refactoring for me. It took a long time. I started writing code in 1981. I first started on that journey towards design only in 1995, after working 5 years as a paid developer. After another 10 years of learning and applying those higher-level techniques, I started to feel a little more comfortable with having an end goal and feeling confident I could craft well-engineered code. It was the practice, reflection and subsequent learning that helped. If you must pick one, pick practice. It all starts from there.

Question: How do software engineers avoid over engineering?
Answer: By just about avoiding under-engineering. It is popular to decry over-engineering, these days. I think that comes - sometimes, on LinkedIn - from attempts to inflate self worth. It’s almost like saying “I am so great at design I can recognise over-engineering!”. It’s not that easy to know where to draw the line, in all honesty. The more serious problem that costs more money (in my opinion) is under-engineering. Untested, unreadable code that somebody threw up and simply said “that should work” then checks it in. WOrk out the cost of untold hours spent trying to pick apart lines of tangled code - that in the end prove to solve only a simple problem. The huge cost increase of adding a feature into a mess of copy-but-not-quite-pasted code. If you’ve ever been in those situations above, you’ll appreciate what a bit of engineering can do for our profession. Putting the Engineer back into Software Engineer. Maybe we need a (not red) MESS hat - “Make Engineered Software Standard” My observation over the years is that the gap between under engineering and over engineering is quite large. You can tolerate a little bit extra better than you can tolerate not enough. It’s not to say that things cannot degenerate into Smart Pattern Soup. They can and they have. But it’s wise to learn what the ‘correct amount’ of engineering is, before making the mistake that any attempt to engineer is too much. Tactics wise, I do my best when I work in tiny micro-steps, writing tests first as executable specifications (of behaviour and programming interface, not implementation), then follow a traditional Red Green Refactor cycle. That gives a strong driver towards having “just enough engineering” on top of otherwise minimalist working code. If that approach is new to you, there are many excellent resources on it. I’ll take the opportunity to plug my Packt book, where we build a microservice with database together using that approach: I’ve found for all but the tiniest of problems, this approach works well. I hope I’ve shown in this answer that this approach is not the only way to do this. The core to it is in the thought process: don’t add things you don’t need, or that do not improve the software. But as Test-First and Software Design are so intimately related, the approach helps more often than not.

Question: What should I expect for the final interview for a junior developer position?

Candidates get the chance to talk about what they are looking for from us. they might find that they don’t want to work with us, or on the kinds of projects we do, or what-have-you. Question: Which performs better if the same developer developed the same website, PHP Laravel, ASP.NET, or Java Spring Boot?
Answer: I’ve been trying to think of a long and useful answer for this, that still fits inside a piece of Quora writing. I can’t. The crux of it is that language does affect runtime performance, but it is not the majority effect in typical web apps. Nor does it always matter. Let’s briefly unpack those two ideas. Performance can be degraded by many things: There are loads of things - loads and loads and loads of things - that affect performance. The magic bullet does not exist. If it did, it most certainly would not be language - despite what the language vendors and fanbois might bleat about. But in the end, language choice does have a last mile effect. The second point is that performance might not matter. The reason is of human origin. With a web app, the end result is for consumption by a human user. Anything that happens within 0.1 second is “fast” to a user. Fast to a CPU is a few picoseconds; a billion times faster. So raw execution speed is often masked by the fact our human cannot process the volume of information our code could spit out. Humans also follow human processes. If you apply for a bank account, we can get back a confirmation that we’ve received your request pretty quick. But it still takes time for some business process to review, check and approve the new account. No amount of swapping out language will speed that up. Things like a payroll run might have one week or one month available to run. As a starting point, it is generally the time taken in fetching data that has the first order effect. Start your performance investigations there. Remember: you do not need things to run as fast as possible. Only fast enough to meet your performance goal - which might be on a slower human time frame.

Question: Are computer science technical interviews (e.g. having applicants solve algorithmic problems in leetcode) actually useful for tech employers? Don’t savvy applicants simply cram-study just for the interviews and then forget everything later anyway?
Answer: Hmm. I have mixed views: yes and no. No - as you say, they are not representative of much in the real world. I can tell you exactly the last time I inverted a binary tree at work - never. Not once in 30 years. You are also right that people will paste in solutions that are not written by themselves into online tests. That is unhelpful as we learn nothing. But also yes. They do test that some low-level fundamental techniques can be applied. They are useful in screening out those who might have a certificate, but literally cannot see that “add up the total cost of a shopping basket” might involve a loop, a collection of items and some way to form a sum. For our early careers applicants (and only those first timers) we use an online coding test provider as that pre screen. But we read the code and ignore the percentage scores, looking for indicators of understanding. It is a bonus if basic good practice in naming and simplicity are followed. The code must also pass its tests - ie write working code. It’s not the leetcode/CS “DSA” style of problem we use, more data and logical problems. So that’s as accessible to all as we can make it on that platform. The more useful next stage is to work together on a problem live. You write a little bit of code to solve a problem before we meet, show and tell, then we try and improve or extend it together. That is much more useful and much more conversation happens, much more information about ability, interest and interpersonal skills emerges. That is much closer to real work. But with many applicants for few places, that first stage “filter out the chancers” is simply a commercial must. Sadly, in many ways. It’s that personal touch that provides the benefit. But it is very expensive to do, both for us and candidates who need to find the time to do all that.

That is precisely how the compiler (or interpreter) understand what the object code must do. Source code includes the suite of automated tests, deployment scripts, and data schema migrations. Tests like these are (or should be) executable specifications of behaviour and intended usage patterns. The other infrastructure as code components explain how the hardware is to be set up and how data is organised. There should be a lot of explanatory information in source code. But … humans. It is easier to write source code that only the compiler understands than it is to write for humans. So no - sometimes the damn code doesn’t seem to mean a thing. And our industry is happy with programmers who write like that.

Question: Is the assertion of Brooks's Law, "adding manpower to a late software project makes it later," still considered accurate, or has it been deemed an exaggeration? If the principle is still valid, what are the reasons behind its continued applicability?

The principle behind it is our inability to predict the future well, combined with our difficulty communicating relevant information Splitting work across a team means making interface contracts that perfectly isolate each work piece. We need to understand the work we need to do in detail. Generally we discover this later as we build for real. The hidden difficulties we never foresaw emerge later, as the unknown unknowns become visible. As people increase, we get too many divisions such that we can not achieve clean splits. Then we trip over each other. To compound the problem, many people assume developing software is manufacturing. Make one widget, hire ten staff, make ten identical widgets. It is not, has never and will never be like this. That independence and repeatability of components and assembly is not there. If you fix these issues, Brooks Law will disappear. You will be the first to do so.

Question: Will software become considerably more secure if rewritten in a memory safe language? Or will the attackers just find a few new ways of exploiting the software?
Answer: Security is one of those multi-faceted things, best thought of as many small probability chains. If an attack is possible via corrupting some memory, it stands to reason that using incorruptible memory will stop that attack vector. The overall probability of attack has been lowered. But by how much? It really doesn’t matter at all if other simple attack vectors exist. Perhaps a faulty 2 factor authentication system means you can more easily just log in, masquerading as a legitimate user. Maybe the memory is safe, but your web interface is full of cross site attack opportunities or SQL injections. Security is about finding out the attack vectors specific to an application. List all technical and social vectors. Prioritise which ones you wish to eliminate or mitigate. Do some work. Building in memory safety - the inability to write to memory where it could cause a problem - is good. Some languages help with this. There are also language independent assists. Some processors help with this. Many operating systems help with this. Various coding standards and safety patterns help with this. There is never one single thing that can fully secure an application - other than delete it.

Question: Did Marconi discover the radio?
Answer: The practical discoverer of radio was Heinrich Hertz[1]. Hertz was testing out some theoretical work by James Clark Maxwell[2], whose equations suggested the idea of electromagnetic waves should exist. Oliver Lodge[3], in 1888 had similar results - an ability to cause a spark remotely, with the mysterious waves providing the power. Special mention to Edward Hughes[4], who detected radio emissions in 1879, but nobody believed a word he was saying. Hertz noticed an odd effect when experimenting with spark gaps. If you made a spark using a Leyden Jar - an early capacitor - across a spark gap of a fixed size, then a spark would be induced in an identical jar a few feet away. Getting a spark with a battery and wires and stuff was understood. But this remote spark? With no battery? He did further experiments and was able to show that whatever it was that was happening, it had properties similar to how light travels. Following that, a lot of engineering work was done. Marconi was certainly a leader of that field - actually getting equipment to make use of this phenomena. Other names that interest me are people like Eduard Branly, who invented a device to make sense of these sparks at the other end. This was a coherer and acted as an early form of AM radio signal demodulator. We’d use a diode (or non linearity of some kind) today. Radio engineering is a field that had many inventors, and eventually investors, working on it at around the same time. It really took off with Lee de Forest[5]’s invention of the Audion[6] thermionic valve (vacuum tube). The Audion could act as a source of radio signals (oscillator), a way to impress voice and music on those signal (modulator), a way to recover that voice and music (demodulator) and a way to make the music loud enough to hear (amplifier). Later valves based on the Audion found use as binary switches - paving the way for automatic telephone exchanges and digital computing. Radio electronics directly led to the modern world.

Question: What are the benefits of Agile project development and dedicated continuous development teams?
Answer: The biggest benefit is stakeholders get value delivered earlier. Fast feedback is the second major benefit. Given many projects, the fact that any value gets delivered at all, ever is a major win. If you follow a traditional waterfall approach, you get 2 years up front of nothing at all. A sheaf of paper. Then, you go live and discover (a) tons of defects based on limited human foresight during plaaning, and (b) half the features are what you asked for, but not what you need. Agile, by contrast, delivers something usable every couple of weeks. Even multiple times a day. At first, it is very limited. Maybe a blank web page - but at least something you can see on your phone. Not a Gantt chart promising that in 2 years. Then you can add the company logo. See it - live. Not a vague promise that is one million pounds and eighteen months away. As features build up to more usable things, real users can validate what we did. Critically, if something isn’t working for them - “we have to press six buttons and sometimes we book in the wrong amount” - then we can adapt our short-term planning to fix that in. At a priority determined by stakeholders. Now, this will not sound like “Agile” to many of you, becuase what you are doing is Wagile - waterfall agile. The planning - architecture, design, feature roadmap, deadlines - are strictly waterfall. But you are allowed to play in an agile-sounding sandpit, full of nice toys like JIRA and standups and scrum masters and velocity charts. None of that shit affects or enables the ability to deliver value and adapt to change quickly. None of it. Zero. Nada. Zip. Zilch. It is waterfall rebadged. You can even mathematically transform burn up charts into Gantt charts if you like (you need burnup data plus a planned task ordering, done). So the trade off is getting valuable software in the hands of users quickly and continuously, or getting paperwork in the hands of stakeholders after a couple of years. Why anybody in their right mind in 2024 champions waterfall, I will never, ever understand. The fun fact? Waterfall is based on a misunderstanding from Winston Royce. He presented the first waterfall diagram as applied to software in 1970: But his accompanying text read: I believe in this concept, but the implementation described above is risky and invites failure….The testing phase which occurs at the end of the development cycle is the first event for which timing, storage, input/output transfers, etc., are experienced as distinguished from analyze. Yet if these phenomena fail to satisfy the various external constraints, then invariably a major redesign is required. Either the requirements must be modified, or a substantial change in the design is required. In effect the development process has returned to the origin and one can expect up to a 100-percent overrun in schedule and/or costs. But hey. Don’t let the “inventor” actually telling you about his failed experiment put you off. That Illusion of Control is a powerful draw.

Question: With the release of Devin (software engineering AI), how will that impact the market?
Answer: Thanks for the answer request. For me, too early to say. Let’s see how it works in the real world, not on the crafted and polished sales demo. There are only ever three outcomes to these gosh-wow AI launches: For me there are two open questions: Point 1 is philosophical. I have no idea. I have not seen anything convincing yet that can - say - create a new scientific theory, apply critical reasoning or even just be left alone to write a large application. Point 2 shows the state of the art as almost disproving a hypothesis that a large enough neural net becomes human like. The latest LLMs are pretty big neural nets already and they are nothing like human level in performance. So what’s my opinion: None. I don;t know enough to predict the future of AI. The present seems massively over-hyped. I see no evidence so far to the contrary. I’m not aware of Devin having any “new approach” leaps to AI, so I guess it’s an iterative refniement of the stuff that doesn’t think. I agree with many people that once a dev in a box machine appears, the whole industry has gone, overnight. You won’t need me - an SWE trainer - to train the developers you don’t employ. They will not be attending the university courses and bootcamps that no longer run. That’s a few trillion quid worth of GDP gone with associated tax drop that will hurt governments in developed countries. That knocks-on to cutting government spending, so about that day care centre you were hoping for, sorry. can’t afford it now. The hope - and likelihood - is that our new army of robocoders will create saleable products that boost this economy. History does show that this is the case. When the spinning jenny inverted cotton spinning economics - from 8 spinners feeding one loom to one spinner feeding 8 looms - we got more stuff. More cloth. More variety. Cheaper sales of clothes and furnishings. That created it’s own new industry of fashion and textile design. That created a market for new kinds of automated machinery. Those machines displaced other manual work, and that cycle increased. See also calculators, tabulators, the internal combustion engine, the Jet, the production line, machine tools. And more. But we also got a load of hand spinners on the dole queue. Time to sell those other skills we all have … (Ah. Bit of a problem. Don;t have any other saleable skills. Oh dear). A robocoder will necessarily mean no more software engineers. We moan too much. We’re too slow. We argue with bosses. We cost loads. Everybody always hated us all anyway, and we are only here as part of a profit centre. So. That. That’s what I think. But it’s all vapid opinion. Other opinions are available.

Question: Why do people still use Java and C++ when there is python?
Answer: Once you’ve got decent at a few languages, you see that each one enables you to see a problem a different way. For any non-trivial code, we will organise that code and separate concerns into smaller blocks. How we do that - which blocks we inevnt - becomes how we explain the problem we are solving to other developers. The lowest level of any code is syntax. That’s the stuff the language provides. The problem domain is the thing we are solving, expressed in human language. Programming is dragging up syntax, kicking and screaming, to that human language level of the problem. Different languages steer you along different paths toward this. This is by design. Python steers a rather different course than either Java or C++. Those two languages are different from each other. You find certain languages allow more straightforward modelling of the problem than others. This seems especially true for small problems. One challenge as we learn programming is that the tools shape our thinking. We not only learn the syntax and application of our first programming language, but we learn how it shapes our view of problems. The second language we learn is a challenge for everybody. It forces us to see problems in a different light. Programming becomes more than rewriting in a new syntax. We end up fighting the language until we discover the new paths towards human problem language the new syntax gives us. So to your question, we often find people stick to their first language for a long time to retain the benefits of that total approach. But other problems have a different feel. Choosing a matching language can help. Commercially, you use the language the existing code is written in, or the majority skill sent the team. Theres nothing fancy about the choice.

Question: How does a fingerprint scanner identify and match fingerprints?
Answer: I was interning at a place that made a fingerprint scanner in the late 1980s. The way that worked then was to decompose the fingerprint image and identify the features called ‘minutiae[1]’. These were reduced to being a vector and a point. The point was the most central part, and the vector gave a direction. One such set of these triples were stored as representing a fingerprint. The scanner would create the same data set for the finger applied and compare the two. An individual’s fingerprint data was stored on the mag stripe of a standard card - as used for a credit card. Authentication involved scanning your finger and swiping the card. There could then be an authorisation step for that individual access point. That system ended up working reasonably well; as I left and went back to university, it hadn’t got to the target levels of false positives and false negatives but was otherwise pretty decent. Impressive kit though and I learned so much by observation. The team built a CCD TV camera plus optics, plus all the electronics to drive that. That was all new (based on a Philips NXA1011 chip). This fed an AMD 29000 CPU (a monster for its time!) and a custom embedded computer based around that. All the graphics processing was really new. Getting the processing time down was a challenge. I expect things have moved on in 40 years.

Question: Is it generally hard for .NET developers to adapt to web technologies and frameworks outside of the .NET environment?
Answer: It should not be - providing that developer has learned the fundamentals behind web development and .NET. If we approach development as a series of step-by-step guides locked to a specific technology, then we don’t really know what we’re doing. We bolt the “widget.NET” to the ‘futzer.NET” and we have no idea why we would do that, only that we get those nice stripes backgrounds if we do. That’s an ok way to work, to a point. We all do in part. But when we take the time to learn how the web works - the HTTP protocol, basic networking, HTML and the DOM - plus the foundations behind programming in general, we see things clearly. The .NET framework - any framework - is a repackaging of the common blocks of code that are mandated by the fundamentals. If we use HTTP, there will always be certain blocks of code to format, send and receive commands. We stick those blocks in frameworks. This means we don’t have to keep re-writing the same block. But it also gives us a new, domain-specific programming language to work with. We learn at a higher level. We can use higher level abstractions than our core programming language offers. That’s the part that needs breaking down and re-building for a new set of tools. The fundamentals have not changed, but the packaging has. We are doing the same old thing in a new domain-specific language, where our “core programming language” (meaning C#, Java, Go, C, Assembler, whatever) is now glue for our domain specific one. That’s the part that can be uncomfortable to unlearn. That’s also the part where you become jaded over the years. “Not that old thing again!”. It feels pointless a few cycles in just learning the ‘new, old’ way of saying the same sentences. It’s painful to watch the fanbois rave about the new way, when there is nothing actually new there. Anyway. Lots of words ending in an old person rant. Yes. It is easily possible to move from one system to another, given a good grasp of fundamentals. It is much harder if you learned by rote. You might not need to, so motivations are key.

Question: Why didn't Hitler invade the UK through the chunnel instead of attempting an amphibious landing?

These would be used to transport soldiers, who would strap in to the shoes for the channel crossing. The amphibians would do the heavy lifting. Question: Coders: Is it really true that to optimize for simplicity, use Python?
Answer: No, it isn’t. You can get simplicity in any popular language. You can also write garbage in any language. Simplicity comes from two things: The first point is about doing easy things in an easy way. Or at least an obvious way. It’s about dividing a large task up into clear smaller tasks, each of which knows very little about how the other tasks work. That leads to a simple design, and simple, uncluttered thinking. Naming is also crucial. Most of a program in any language is made up of names that the programmer chooses. A small fraction of that program is made up from actual language syntax and keywords. Names are where we describe our bigger ideas and bigger building blocks in our program. By revealing intent in our naming, we simplify the transfer of knowledge. If we are adding funds to a bank account, let’s see the words “add”, “funds” and “account” rather than anything obscure. We can name functions and methods by what they will have done for us once they complete. We can name variables by what piece of information they hold. Python is one of the easiest languages to start writing with. But for large applications, it starts to lose that clarity. the things “Python does all for you” start to represent a loss of engineering information, rather than the saving of a few keystrokes. It’s a popular, and decent choice for a beginner language. It is widely used in commercial development. But it would be a mistake to think that simplicity is guaranteed when using Python, or indeed that simplicity comes from any language choice. Simplicity comes from clear thinking, expressed clearly.

Question: Why would a Java developer use a non-static method so that class instantiation is required to access and call the method?
Answer: Because Java is designed to force you into using objects for everything. The neatest, least verbose syntax will come from using objects. There’s nothing inherently wrong (in my view) with an object that has a single method, and that does not have any state associated with it. We often find that such an object becomes a “behaviour attractor” - meaning that later on, it might grow some state. It might not. Either way it is still an object, encapsulating some logic. The static keyword really is to do with collections of objects. Static means that a method has no direct connection with a ‘this’ pointer - it has no sense of self identity. But it will have access to any private members of such an object passed into it as a parameter. So a static method can operate effectively over a collection of objects, more or less as a function would. To many people, including the Java designers theselves, this is used to emulate a standalone function. Java works hard to make you avoid standalone functions. It really does prefer you to use object instances. I avoid using static methods to emulate functions. I just use an object instance. It seems more direct and honest in the Java language. There’s not much in it either way in terms of source code. against There is a chance that the object version will grow a reason to have state. You could easily refactor it to this: and this becomes interesting once we do a bit of method chaining and so on. You start to grow out a useful OOP “utils” class (ugh) which might even become more domain specific over time. Doing this with chained static methods is clunkier. You can then pass around an object instance of the Strings class and inject it into things if you like, with a simple syntax. By contrast, the static function drags around lambda syntax which gets clunky in the receiver sometimes. And you still cannot have a proper function, even with lambdas (they are single-method anonymous classes under the covers) Whatever I say, though, there is an awful lot of static method as a C function style coding about, even in the JDK standard libraries. It tends to encourage procedural thinking, which itself moves against the sweet spot of Java with its “objects for everything” goal.

Question: Did you know that C++ is statistically almost twice slower than C because it needs additional code to handle exceptions, dynamic pointers and classes?
Answer: Utter rubbish I’m afraid. What happens here is people don’t compare like for like. They might say a virtual function is slower than a C function. Correct. But a virtual function is not used to replace a C function. Instead, it replaces a set of C functions with a switch on a type code, to decide which function to run (or, alternately function pointers). That’s the same cpu opcodes and the same run time. I think noobs need to learn a bit more in their silent phase before making bold, wrong claims.

Question: How do I start developing a software framework?
Answer: Apologies for the well below standard GPT paste-ins you have received. Frameworks are hard enough to design that whole books have been written on this subject. This is your best bet The basics of creating a framework are: Once the variations are known, you can revise the concrete code to be more flexible: This is now the first pass of your framework. One piece of reusable code can support two different applications. As an example, let’s make a UI button. It needs to say “Click me” and pop up an alert box. We code that up hard-coded. To generalise, we pass the text to display to the button component. We also supply a callback function. This will be called when we click the button. At this point, our button code knows nothing about its text, nor what code runs when we click it. It has become independent of either application, and can support both - plus new ones in future. This idea of “externalising variation” is core to frameworks. The whole idea of plug-in systems is the same. Many libraries are written this way. Where a framework really comes in to play is when it gets opinionated. Certain decisions are made by the framework designer - to remove work from you - but you must comply with their approach. As an example, let’s say we to create a toy framework that will run all applications. We won’t need to write our own ‘main’ function. To do this, our framework would provide the programmer an interface that must be implemented: You would write an implementation that provided your code for each method - one to initialise() your app, the other to run() it. The framework would provide a way to bind your specific code: Once done, the framework can then call your initialise() method followed by your run ()method. You don’t get to make those calls. You don’t choose what order they happen in. The framework designer makes those decisions. You just comply. This is known as ‘the Hollywood Principle’ in frameworks - “don’t call us; we’ll call you”. That’s all a framework is. Common code between applications separated from application-specific code, using the Dependency Inversion Principle of SOLID. Start small and write a practice mini-framework!

Question: Should one know coding in order to work in AWS DevOps? Do they actually create code and apps?

Question: How much force is required to lift the weight of your 100kg?
Answer: 100kg is a measure of mass, strictly, not weight. The amount of force to lift a mass depends on the strength of gravity pulling that mass down. On earth, 100kg mass weighs 981 Newtons. So you need a pulling force of a bit more than 981 newtons to lift it up. On the moon, with one sixth of the gravity pull, you’d need six times less force.

Question: Why is it that most software Engineering projects have no requirements for producing complex algorithms or heavy mathematics?
Answer: Software reflects the real world problem we are solving. If you are writing microcontroller code to flash a car turn indicator, there’s no complex algorithm If you are adding up the marks for an online quiz, you’re using basic addition. If you are storing some basic user profile data in some store somewhere, it is a call to store data. There are lots of things we do in the real world that simply are not complex. When we automate a not complex thing, it is not complex. Unless we make a total hash of it, something called “adding accidental complexity”. Some algorithms are complex, to solve complex real-world problems. Depends entirely what you are working on.
